Summary

AstraSync must decide whether to accept one of the client’s two lower-priced counteroffers (A: $152K per month; B: $125K per month plus an $800K success bonus) or reject both and compete in an RFP at $150K per month plus a gain-share reward (C). We valued each option as the present value of AstraSync’s contribution over 18 months at a 1.5% monthly rate, built a decision tree, and ran 1,000,000 Monte Carlo draws of the triangular client-savings distribution to value the gain-share. On expected value the three options are nearly tied: C at $509,329, B at $506,713 and A at $501,522. C’s lead of about $2,616 disappears if the chance of winning the RFP falls below 39.8% (the team’s estimate is 40%), and C leaves a 60% chance of earning nothing. We recommend AstraSync accept Option B, giving up less than 1% of expected value to keep the account and avoid the all-or-nothing RFP.

The three alternatives

Option A: equal payments of $152,000 per month. AstraSync’s cost is 1,200 hours × $100 = $120,000 per month, so A earns a certain $32,000 per month. Discounted over 18 months at 1.5%, that is $501,522 with no risk at all.

Option B: $125,000 per month plus an $800,000 bonus at month 18. The monthly margin is only $5,000 (PV $78,363), but the bonus is paid if the implementation beats the client’s benchmark, which AstraSync puts at 70%. The bonus is worth $611,929 in today’s dollars, so the outcomes are $690,292 (70%) or $78,363 (30%), for an expected $506,713.

Option C: reject both and bid $150,000 per month in the RFP. If AstraSync wins (40%), it earns $30,000 per month (PV $470,177) plus a gain-share at month 18 that depends on the client’s savings, Triangular($3.2M, $5.6M, $12.8M). The simulated mean gain-share is $1,049,984 (PV $803,145), so winning is worth $1,273,322. Losing (60%) earns $0. Expected value: $509,329.

Expected value is not the whole story
Option Expected value Worst outcome Best outcome Chance of $0
A $501,522 $501,522 $501,522 0%
B $506,713 $78,363 $690,292 0%
C $509,329 $0 $3,589,839 60%

The expected values sit within about $7,807 of each other, but the spread of outcomes is very different. A is certain; B has a floor of $78,363; C is the only option where AstraSync can walk away with nothing, which it does in 6 of 10 cases.

Input 1: probability of winning the RFP
Input 2: probability of earning the Option B bonus
Where the recommendation flips
  • P(win RFP): C beats B only above 39.8%. The team’s 40% estimate sits just 0.21 percentage points above that edge, so a slightly pessimistic view of the competition flips the ranking to B.
  • P(bonus): B beats A whenever the bonus probability exceeds 69.2% and beats C above 70.4%. The 70% estimate sits between the two, again within about one point of each edge.
  • RFP bid: C ties B at a bid of $149,583 per month. Shaving even about $500 off the $150K bid to beat competitors erases C’s advantage.
Conclusion

Accept Option B. Strictly by expected value, the RFP (C) ranks first at $509,329, followed by B at $506,713 and A at $501,522, but the gap between first and second is about $2,616, well inside the uncertainty of the inputs that produce it.

The sensitivity analysis shows how fragile C’s lead is: it depends on a 40% win probability that only has to drop to 39.8% to lose its edge, and on bidding a full $150K per month in a competitive RFP. C also carries a 60% chance of earning nothing and losing the client relationship.

Option B keeps the account, guarantees a positive contribution of at least $78,363, and pays $690,292 in the 70% case where AstraSync’s confidence in its own delivery is justified. It also aligns AstraSync’s pay with the client’s results, which supports the director’s goal of growing the relationship.

What would change our mind: evidence that AstraSync’s chance of winning the RFP is clearly above 40% (for example, few credible competitors), or a bonus probability below 69.2%, at which point the certain $152K per month of Option A becomes the better choice.
